claims.text: The target alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The target material is a defect-free polycrystal with no extended defects, no significant dislocation density, and an average grain size of approximately 10 µm.
The predictive model combines DFT phonon dispersions, explicit mass- and force-constant-disorder scattering, and ab initio Boltzmann electron transport.
Atomic mass and force-constant disorder arise from size and mass mismatch among Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr.
Mass and force-constant disorder enhance phonon scattering.
DFT-computed phonon linewidths capture the enhanced phonon scattering caused by alloy disorder.
Ab initio Boltzmann transport adequately treats alloy-disorder electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
The model will predict lattice thermal conductivity within ±10% of experiment over 100–1200 K.
The model will predict electronic thermal conductivity within ±15% of experiment over 100–1200 K.
The model will predict total thermal conductivity within ±12% across 100–1200 K.
The model will reduce total-conductivity prediction error by approximately 20% compared with existing Debye-based analytical methods.
At 300 K, the model predicts total thermal conductivity of 12 ± 1.5 W/(m·K).
Previously reported total thermal conductivity for HfNbTaTiZr is 10–17 W/(m·K).
Debye-temperature models coupled to DFT elastic constants have approximately 30% error for HfNbTaTiZr thermal-conductivity predictions.
The model is applicable to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr polycrystals with oxygen content up to 1 wt.%, grain size of at least 1 µm, and negligible dislocation density.
Mass-disorder-parameter uncertainty produces approximately ±3% uncertainty near 300 K.
Neglected higher-order anharmonicity produces up to ±10% uncertainty near 1200 K.
Magnetic-field 3ω measurements can separate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions over 10–200 K.
Thermal-conductivity, Hall-effect, and electrical-resistivity measurements can deconvolute electronic and lattice thermal transport over 300–800 K.
A deviation greater than 15% for either predicted lattice or electronic thermal conductivity in a low- or high-temperature regime falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis, initial state, and conditions require oxygen content ≤0.1 wt.%, whereas the boundary expands applicability to ≤1 wt.% without explanation.
The material is described as a polycrystal with finite grain size while also being defect-free and having no extended defects; polycrystalline grain boundaries are extended defects.

The hypothesis promises ±10% accuracy for κ_L and ±12% for total conductivity, but the falsification rule only rejects κ_L or κ_e deviations greater than 15%. Thus some outcomes that violate the stated accuracy claims would not falsify the hypothesis under its own rule, and no explicit falsification threshold is given for total conductivity.

Applicability is limited to 100–1200 K, but the low-temperature falsification regime extends down to 10 K and is said to falsify the hypothesis without restricting the comparison to temperatures at or above 100 K.
